case.title: The Canal Hum
case.hook: The Gazette asked me to find a mystery hum. Rule number one of sound: something has to be vibrating. Let’s find out what, and how the sound gets inside those houses.

paper.name: The Palmetto Beach Gazette
paper.headline: Mystery hum keeps canal neighbors awake
paper.deck: A low sound starts after dark. Nobody can find where it comes from.

body: Every night this winter, families along Pelican Canal hear a low hum. It starts after sunset and keeps going past midnight.
“It sounds like a big truck waiting outside,” said one neighbor. “But nothing is there.”
Some neighbors say they can FEEL it buzzing in their walls and floors. The Gazette asked engineer Sam Park to find the source.

letters.t: It must be a ship’s engine way out in the bay.
My cousin says it’s a generator. Or ghosts!
In my yard it is quiet. Inside my house by the water, the walls hum.

case.question: What is making the canal hum, and how does it get into the houses?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.where: Warm-Up: hold it to stop it
clues.t: Every sound comes from something vibrating. Stop the vibration, and the sound stops. So something near the canal is vibrating.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: be the vibration
clues.t: Sound is a vibration passed along as a wave. Air, water and even walls just shake in place and pass the push along.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: match the note
clues.t: Slow vibrations make a LOW pitch. Fast vibrations make a HIGH pitch. The hum is low, so its source vibrates slowly.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: the ruler test
clues.t: The longer the ruler, the slower it vibrated and the lower it sounded. A low hum comes from a slow vibration.

solve.title: What is making the canal hum?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: A ship’s engine far out in the bay, sending tiny sound balls through the air.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Sound isn’t tiny balls flying. And the hum is loudest by the canal, inside the houses.

options.t: Something in the canal water vibrating slowly. Its low waves travel through the water, the ground and the walls into the houses.
options.why: Case cracked! Something in the water vibrates slowly (a low pitch), and the waves travel through water, ground and walls. Meet the hum-maker just below!

options.t: A very LOUD sound, because loud sounds are always low.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Loudness is how BIG a vibration is. Pitch is how FAST. A whistle can be loud AND high.

options.t: Nothing is vibrating. Some sounds just happen by themselves.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Every sound starts with something vibrating.

todo: Press “Make it ring” on a picture.

holdstop.q: What did your hand really stop?

opts.t: The vibration. No vibration, no sound.
The sound flying out of it.
opts.miss: Did anything fly out? What did your hand feel, and stop?
Light doesn’t make sound. What was the thing doing before you held it?

holdstop.win: No vibration, no sound. Something by the canal must be vibrating. Clue 1!

wiggle.title: Be the vibration
todo: Drag left and right, again and again, in the orange strip (or press a wiggle button).
Watch the dots pass the push to the ear. Keep your eye on the red dot.
Send the sound through air, canal water and a house wall.

why.t: A model of the tiny bits that air, water and walls are made of. They’re much too small to see.

wiggle.redLine: The red dot is one bit of air. Does it reach the ear?
wiggle.dragLine: Drag here: left, right, left, right!
wiggle.pathLabel: What is the sound moving through?
wiggle.heardWord: The eardrum is shaking: you hear it!

paths.note: In air, the bits are far apart. The push moves slowest here.
In water, the bits are packed closer. The push moves about 4 times faster than in air.
In solid wood or concrete, the push moves even faster. A hum from outside can make a wall buzz.

tasks.paths: Send it through air, water and a wall

wiggle.q: Look at the red dot. Did it travel to the ear?

opts.t: No. It only rocked back and forth and passed the push along.
Yes. It flew all the way to the ear.
opts.miss: Watch the red dot again. Does it ever get to the ear?
Look again. The red dot is still there. What is it doing?

wiggle.win: Sound is a vibration passed along, not a flying thing. And it moves through water and walls, too. Clue 2!

tuner.afterText: Try to tune one by ear
tuner.title: Match the note
todo: Press “Play the target note” and listen.
Make the band shorter or longer, looser or tighter. Then pluck it.
Match all 3 notes by ear. The counter shows how fast it vibrates.

why.t: A rubber band works like a guitar string. It’s an easy way to see what changes the pitch.

tuner.lowLine: Too LOW: it vibrates too slowly. Make it vibrate faster.
tuner.highLine: Too HIGH: it vibrates too fast. Make it vibrate slower.
tuner.r2Line: Pluck it gently, then hard. Watch the counter.

opts.miss: Look at the counter. Did the vibrations each second change?
Look at the counter. Did the vibrations each second change?

tuner.q: How do you make a HIGHER pitch?

opts.t: Make it vibrate faster: shorter or tighter.

opts.miss: Harder made it louder. Did the counter go up?
Try it! Did the pitch go up or down?

tuner.win: Fast = high. Slow = low. A big swing = loud. The canal hum is low, so its source vibrates slowly. Clue 3!

rulerlab.afterText: how much hangs off the edge, and listen
rulerlab.title: The ruler test
todo: Pick how much ruler hangs over the edge: 2, 6 or 10 inches.
Drag the red tip down and let go (or press Pluck it). Listen.
Pick the pitch you heard. Fill all 3 rows of the table.

why.t: If you change only the length, you know the length is what changed the pitch. That makes it a fair test.

rulerlab.lenLabel: How much hangs over the edge?

missPitch.high: Listen again. A short ruler twangs very fast. Was it a high buzz or a low thwap?
missPitch.mid: Listen again. Compare it with the other lengths. Is it in the middle?
missPitch.low: Listen again. A long ruler flaps slowly: thwap, thwap. High or low?

rulerlab.pitchQ: What pitch did you hear at {L} inches?
rulerlab.pullLine: Drag the red tip down and let go, or press Pluck it.
rulerlab.slowLine: (The picture is slowed way down so you can see it.)

opts.t: The length hanging off. Shorter → faster vibrations → higher pitch.

opts.miss: Plucking harder makes it louder. Look at your table: what did you change?
The ruler never changed color! What did you change?

rulerlab.win: Shorter = faster = higher. Longer = slower = lower. A deep hum means a slow vibration. Clue 4!

drumfish.title: Meet the black drum
todo: Look at the real fish.
Press Play to hear a model of their night chorus.
drumfish.lockLine: Crack the case first. Then meet the hum-maker.
drumfish.alt: A young black drum fish with dark stripes and small whiskers under its chin.
drumfish.cap: A young black drum. Its stripes fade as it grows. See the little whiskers (barbels) under its chin? They help it feel for food.
drumfish.credit: Black drum (Pogonias cromis): Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

facts.t: Black drum are big fish that live in Florida’s bays, rivers and canals. Big ones can weigh more than 50 pounds.
To drum, a special muscle squeezes the fish’s swim bladder (an air-filled bag inside it) again and again, very fast. The bladder vibrates like a drum.
They drum at night in winter and early spring, when they gather to lay eggs. The sound is LOW and very strong.
This really happened in Florida! In canals in Cape Coral and Punta Gorda, people heard black drum inside their homes. Scientists found them with hydrophones (underwater microphones).

drumfish.playBtn: ▶ Play a model of the night chorus
drumfish.chorusLine: Made with computer sounds. It’s a model, not a real recording.
drumfish.win: Mystery solved: the hum was fish! A vibrating muscle, a low pitch, and waves through water, ground and walls.

causes.t: Black drum fish drumming in the canal
causes.say: The hum comes from black drum fish in the canal. A muscle squeezes each fish’s swim bladder, and the bladder vibrates.

causes.miss: Then the hum would be loudest out in the bay. Where is it loudest?
Fun idea! But what does every sound need?

evidence.t: The hum is LOW, so its source vibrates slowly.
Sound waves travel through water, ground and walls, so walls can buzz.
It starts after dark, when black drum gather to lay eggs.
Sound is made of tiny balls.
evidence.miss: Check Clue 2. Is sound a flying thing?

column.win: Printed! Pelican Canal knows the truth: the neighbors are fish.

why.q: Why do the bands sound different?
why.t: Each band is a different length. Shorter bands vibrate faster and sound higher.

tool.name: Hydrophone
tool.teaser: Drop an underwater microphone into the bay and the canal. When and where is the hum?
tool.done: You listened at every spot. A hydrophone sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A microphone that works underwater. Sound travels well in water, so scientists use hydrophones to listen to fish, whales and ships.

todo: Tap a spot to drop the hydrophone in.
Watch the wave and listen.
Try all 3 spots.

hydrophone.cap: A diver checks a hydrophone on the sea floor at Gray’s Reef National Marine Sanctuary, Georgia.
hydrophone.credit: Photo: NOAA National Marine Sanctuaries (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons.

spots.read: Crackle, crackle: HIGH clicks, fairly quiet.
spots.note: That’s snapping shrimp, tiny shrimp that snap their claws shut. Lots of short, high sounds.

spots.read: Almost quiet: a faint, low hum of a boat far away.
spots.note: Small, slow waves on the screen. No mystery hum during the day.

spots.read: BOOM-boom-boom: LOW and LOUD. Tall, slow waves.
spots.note: Lots of low knocks at once, like a crowd of drums. That’s the hum!

q.q: Where and when is the hum?

opts.why: Yes! Real scientists in Cape Coral and Punta Gorda used hydrophones the same way to find the black drum chorus.

opts.t: In the open bay, at noon.
opts.miss: Those were high crackles. Is the hum high or low?
Compare the canal at noon and at 9 PM. Was it the same?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain what sound is, or why high notes sound different?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Every sound starts with a vibration, and faster vibrations make a higher pitch.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “sound”, “vibration”, “faster” and “higher pitch”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
